note.text: Economies of scale occur when larger output scale lowers long-run average cost as the firm can vary all inputs. Internal economies arise within the firm, such as specialisation, technical indivisibilities or purchasing advantages. External economies can arise from an industry’s expansion, such as specialised suppliers or a relevant skills pool. Total cost can rise while average cost falls. A purchasing discount is useful only if storage, quality and demand make the larger order worthwhile. Size does not guarantee a cost saving.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain why larger scale can lower long-run average cost and calculate the saving per unit. Builds on: resources, finance and the cost of supplying output. Leads to: diseconomies of scale and the limits to expansion.

sections.heading: Understand the economics
sections.text: Economies of scale occur when larger output scale lowers long-run average cost as the firm can vary all inputs. Internal economies arise within the firm, such as specialisation, technical indivisibilities or purchasing advantages. External economies can arise from an industry’s expansion, such as specialised suppliers or a relevant skills pool. Total cost can rise while average cost falls. A purchasing discount is useful only if storage, quality and demand make the larger order worthwhile. Size does not guarantee a cost saving.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: A fictional Douala workshop compares complete production plans at different scales. Specialist equipment may spread its services over more output, and a larger firm may organise specialised tasks. A cluster of firms can also support a specialist supplier. These are possible mechanisms, not proof that every large firm is efficient or every observed cost fall comes from scale.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Compute average cost as total cost divided by comparable output. State whether the cause is internal to one firm or external through its industry. Separate long-run scale from a short-run change with fixed capacity. Lower cost may enable lower prices, but the actual price also depends on market conditions.

key_words.meaning: a scale-related cost advantage arising within the firm
a benefit linked to expansion of the industry or cluster rather than one firm alone
total cost divided by the corresponding output
a scale-related opportunity to obtain inputs on lower unit-cost terms

mistake.wrong: Every internal economy comes only from unrelated firms expanding.
mistake.right: internal economy: a scale-related cost advantage arising within the firm.
mistake.why: The source is within the expanding firm’s own organisation or technology.

worked_example.problem: Compare a smaller long-run plan costing {10000} for {20} units with a larger plan costing {16000} for {40} units.
steps: Average costs: {10000/20} and {16000/40} CFA francs per unit.
The larger plan saves {10000/20-16000/40} per unit even though its total cost is higher.
worked_example.answer: Average cost falls by {10000/20-16000/40} CFA francs per unit.

cards.idea: Distinguish these features before judging a business.
example: internal economy: a scale-related cost advantage arising within the firm.
external economy: a benefit linked to expansion of the industry or cluster rather than one firm alone.
average cost: total cost divided by the corresponding output.
purchasing economy: a scale-related opportunity to obtain inputs on lower unit-cost terms.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: The firm can justify specialised equipment as its scale expands.
Industry growth supports a specialised local supplier used by several firms.
The workshop compares cost per unit rather than total spending alone.
A larger appropriate order may obtain better input terms.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.

external economy: The benefit arises from the industry environment, not that personal work change.
average cost: Output may rise faster than total cost, reducing average cost.
purchasing economy: Storage, spoilage and demand can offset the apparent input-price saving.
